findings.reason: The authenticated source guarantees uniqueness only for complete [username, timestamp, website] tuples; timestamp values themselves may tie. The protected and immutable native sources globally sort records, discard timestamps, and then combine positions, so they can manufacture an order between same-time visits. On the legal log username = [u,u,u,u], timestamp = [1,1,2,3], website = [a,b,z,z], both return [a,b,z], whose first two visits are simultaneous, while the strict-time oracle and candidate correctly return [a,z,z].

candidate.py keeps each timestamp attached to its website, sorts histories independently per user, and filters tied histories with the explicit condition first_time < second_time < third_time. A concise all-distinct fast path delegates ordinary three-site generation to itertools.combinations without weakening the tied-timestamp rule. histories, visits, sites, timestamps_are_distinct, patterns, scores, and best clearly expose the data flow; no unnecessary helper or abstraction obscures the interview algorithm.

Every retained triple has strictly increasing visit times and therefore forms a chronological three-site pattern, including repeated names and nonconsecutive visits. Conversely, any user who matches a pattern supplies one such triple. Converting each user's triples to a set limits that user to one score contribution per pattern, Counter aggregates distinct users, and minimizing (-score, pattern) applies the maximum-score rule and full lexicographic tie-break together.

Metadata consistently identifies Premium LeetCode algorithm problem 1152, Python, and native entrypoint Solution.mostVisitedPattern. Authenticated evidence confirms three aligned arrays of length 3 through 50, lowercase names of length 1 through 10, timestamps from 1 through 10^9, unique complete visit tuples, at least one user with three visits, nonconsecutive ordered patterns with repeated sites allowed, distinct-user scoring, and lexicographic tie resolution. The candidate preserves solve(username, timestamp, website) and the three-string list result.

The immutable native source remains byte-for-byte bound to verified submission 2067856998, and the protected source and submission manifest are unchanged. The inert candidate retains the Accepted solution's per-user chronology, three-visit combination generation, user-local set deduplication, global score counter, and final composite selection key, while retaining timestamps long enough to repair the uncovered source-legal tie condition. No remote-verification claim is made for the candidate.

Grouping and sorting all records costs O(m log m) in the worst case. For user u, both the direct and tie-filtered paths inspect at most choose(l_u, 3) visit triples, so the total generation work is O(C). Histories, per-user pattern sets, and the global counter use O(m + C) space. The candidate therefore meets the Optimal branch's O(m log m + C) time and O(m + C) space requirements.

The unchanged hidden tiers scale one distinct-site history from 6 through 12 to 24 visits, a 4x span that exercises cubic combination generation. The exact candidate passed every ordinary and benchmark output and scaling with a 1.06x largest runtime ratio and -0.08 extra growth exponent. An independently correct correlated-rescan control passed every output but failed only scaling with a 44.49x largest ratio and +1.97 relative growth exponent. benchmark.json required no edit.

It derives the declared bounds from m and C and covers timestamp ties, repeated names, nonconsecutive visits, duplicate formations by one user, unsorted input, and score ties.
